content: The study by Wilkinson et al. (2009) in The Lancet highlights the public health benefits of strategies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in the context of household energy use. Establishing clear standards for technology performance, quality, and impact assessment is essential for improving the effectiveness of clean cooking solutions. These standards provide a common framework for communication, understanding, and enhancing the performance of such technologies. They also serve as a practical means of implementing health-based guidelines by setting specific, measurable targets for certification, regulation, and labeling. Consumers depend on these standards to make informed decisions, while designers and manufacturers use them to validate product quality and drive innovation. Policymakers, donors, and investors can leverage these standards to compare stove performance and quality credibly. Furthermore, standards help translate ambitious, evidence-based guidelines into actionable targets that align with stakeholder priorities and can be achieved progressively over time. The process of developing standards is inclusive and consensus-driven, ensuring buy-in from diverse stakeholder groups. These standards must be feasible for the private sector, address consumer needs, and push the sector toward goals such as those outlined in the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. Cooking practices and cuisines vary globally, but international harmonization of standards facilitates the sharing of information on stove and device performance. An international standards process allows countries to collaborate on standards relevant to their national contexts, requiring minimal adaptation for local adoption. The Global Alliance for Clean Cookstoves (GACC) has been instrumental in developing international standards, ensuring participation from a wide range of stakeholders across multiple countries. The GACC has partnered with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), which provides transparent, consensus-based processes for drafting and approving standards in the clean cooking sector. The development of the International Workshop Agreement (IWA) in 2012 marked a significant milestone in global efforts to establish standards for clean cookstoves and fuels. This agreement, developed through collaboration among over 90 stakeholders from 23 countries, introduced a tiered framework for evaluating cookstove performance based on four key indicators: efficiency, total emissions, indoor emissions, and safety. The IWA framework allows for recognition of progress (from Tier 0 as a baseline) while setting aspirational goals (Tier 4). It also provides flexibility for organizations and countries to prioritize indicators based on local needs and enables harmonization of different testing protocols used globally. The ISO Technical Committee 285, established in 2013, is tasked with formalizing these standards. Kenya and the United States serve as co-secretariats of this committee, which includes participation from 20 countries, 14 observing nations, and seven international liaison organizations, including WHO. Drafting and approval of standards are conducted through expert working groups within the committee. The IWA framework is being updated to reflect new findings, including those from WHO guidelines, and to incorporate additional methodologies and indicators. Testing is a critical component of technology development, enabling the evaluation of stove performance against established standards and their potential to meet indoor air quality guidelines. Both laboratory and field testing are necessary, as they provide complementary insights into technology performance under controlled and real-world conditions. However, more testing capacity is needed, particularly in developing countries where household air pollution from solid fuel use is a significant concern. Efforts are underway to establish regional testing and knowledge centers (RTKCs) to provide high-quality testing services and catalyze regional activities. These centers aim to standardize methods, establish best practices, and share testing results through common data formats. The clean cooking sector has made substantial progress in protocol development and standardization, particularly through the ongoing ISO TC 285 process. Emerging protocols are being developed to evaluate the robustness of technologies under various usage conditions and to better reflect actual in-home use. Additionally, carbon finance has driven significant activity in the sector, with methodologies for evaluating health and climate impacts being harmonized to support investment and policy decisions. Regulation and certification mechanisms are essential for implementing and enforcing standards, as well as for communicating technology quality and performance to users. Standards can be used to regulate locally manufactured or imported technologies, with the potential for stricter requirements over time as more advanced technologies become available. Effective labeling depends on clear presentation of information, consumer awareness campaigns, and enforcement to prevent counterfeiting. Studies are needed to evaluate the impact of labeling on consumer decisions and to optimize label design. In summary, the development and implementation of standards for clean cooking technologies are critical for reducing the health burden associated with household air pollution. These efforts also contribute to broader societal, environmental, and climate benefits. The guidelines and standards are targeted at public health policymakers and specialists working across sectors to develop and implement policies that mitigate the adverse health impacts of household fuel combustion. WHO and its partners continue to provide technical support, monitor progress, and evaluate the impact of these initiatives.
